lessons.title: Du solltest mehr schlafen: sollte for advice
lessons.goal: Name a learning problem and give a friendly piece of advice with sollte: sollte in position 2, the infinitive at the end, nicht before the infinitive.

grammar.point: Sollte (Konjunktiv II) gives friendly advice: ich sollte, du solltest, er/sie/es sollte (no umlaut). It works like a modal verb: sollte in position 2, the infinitive at the end, nicht before the infinitive. Time words like früher or gestern show the past meaning (was supposed to). Soll means someone else wants it now.

mistake.why: Sollte works like a modal verb: the infinitive goes to the very end of the sentence, after everything else.

terms.meaning: the soft verb form for advice and polite requests; you know könnte, now sollte
friendly should: Du solltest mehr schlafen
with sollte the second verb waits at the end of the sentence

cards.title: Before we start: from „Du kannst …“ to „Du solltest …“
cards.body: Ben has an exam in two weeks. He cannot concentrate, he forgets words and he starts too late. In the WG Mira and Anna want to help him. You already give small tips with kannst and könntest. Today you learn the friendliest word for advice: sollte. This whole chapter is about learning: problems, advice, courses and exams.
steps: You already know: Könntest du …? (from chapter 5), Du kannst den Bus nehmen (an idea for a friend), and modal verbs with the infinitive at the end.
New today: sollte for advice (Du solltest mehr schlafen), words for learning problems, and how it differs from soll.
By the end you can: name a learning problem and give a friend one friendly piece of advice.

examples.en: Could you help me?
examples.why: You know this already: könnte for a polite question.

examples.en: You can take the bus.
examples.why: You know this already: kannst + infinitive at the end.

examples.en: You should sleep more.
examples.why: New today: solltest is friendly advice.

cards.more: Picture two friends on a sofa. Ben says: I am so tired, I cannot learn. Friend one says Du musst schlafen! That sounds like a parent giving an order. Friend two says Du solltest mehr schlafen. That sounds like a kind tip with a smile. Today you learn to be friend two. Good news: the sentence is built like Du kannst den Bus nehmen. You only swap kannst for solltest, and the second verb still waits at the end.

cards.title: Ben has a Lernproblem: words for learning
cards.body: Ben studies a lot but nothing sticks. His Konzentration is bad, his Gedächtnis forgets words and he has little Motivation. He puts things off (aufschieben) and has too little Lernzeit. Mira says: look the word up (nachschlagen) and write it in your Vokabelheft. Ask Anna for a Lerntipp, and give Ben a good Ratschlag.
cards.lead: Before you can advise someone, you need the problem. This card gives the words of the lesson in simple present-tense sentences about Ben's week.

examples.en: Ben cannot concentrate.
examples.why: Konzentration: the noun; konzentrieren: the verb.

examples.en: He forgets the words.
He puts everything off.

deeper.text: Aufschieben and nachschlagen are separable verbs. In the present the small part goes to the end: Er schiebt alles auf. Ich schlage das Wort nach. In the infinitive they stay in one piece: aufschieben, nachschlagen. Nachschlagen is also irregular: er schlägt nach (a becomes ä).

example.de: Ben schlägt das Wort nach.
example.en: Ben looks the word up.

cards.more: Think of a doctor. Before giving any medicine, the doctor first asks: where does it hurt? Learning problems are the same. Before you can give a tip, you need words for what is wrong: no Konzentration, a bad Gedächtnis, no Motivation, too little Lernzeit. Then come the words for the fix: nachschlagen, a Vokabelheft, a Lerntipp, a Ratschlag. Say every noun with its article, out loud, twice: der Ratschlag, das Gedächtnis. The article is part of the word, like a surname.

cards.title: Sollte: the friendly „should“
cards.body: Sollte gives friendly advice. It works like a modal verb you know: sollte is in position 2 and the second verb stands at the END in the infinitive. You know the same idea from könnte in chapter 5. Sollte sounds soft: it is a tip, not an order. The subject can be du, a name or a person like Ben.
cards.lead: You can name the problem. Now you give the advice: one new verb form, built exactly like a modal sentence you already know.

examples.en: You should sleep more.
Ben should start earlier.
Mira should take a break.

deeper.text: Careful with English: we say you ought to sleep, with to. German never puts zu after sollte. Du solltest zu schlafen is wrong; the infinitive stands alone at the end, just like after kannst or musst. You can also make the tip softer with vielleicht (maybe) right after the verb. This is a common way to soften a tip.

example.de: Du solltest vielleicht mehr Wasser trinken.
example.en: Maybe you should drink more water.

cards.more: English and German do this almost the same way. English says: you should sleep more. German says: du solltest mehr schlafen. The only big difference is the place of the second verb. In English, sleep stands right after should. In German, schlafen walks to the very end of the sentence, behind mehr, früher or eine Pause. Imagine the infinitive is a shy guest who always sits in the last chair. Everything else sits between sollte and that last chair.
steps: Subject: Du / Ben / Mira
sollte / solltest in position 2
The rest: mehr, früher, eine Pause
Infinitive at the END: schlafen, anfangen, machen

cards.title: Ich sollte, du solltest, er sollte: the forms
cards.body: The forms are easy: ich sollte, du solltest, er/sie/es sollte. Ich and er are the same, like in the past of modal verbs. Watch the spelling: sollte has NO umlaut, unlike könnte. It is not söllte. With ich, sollte often means: I really should do this (advice to myself).
cards.lead: Now look at the three forms side by side. Seeing them next to soll and könnte will keep the spelling clear.

examples.en: I should study now.
You should look up the word.
He should sleep early today.

deeper.text: Native speakers often add eigentlich (actually) to ich sollte. Ich sollte eigentlich lernen means: I really ought to study, but I am not doing it. It is the classic sentence of a tired learner at night, and it often goes on with aber. So ich sollte is not only advice for others; it is also a small, honest complaint about yourself.

example.de: Ich sollte eigentlich lernen, aber ich bin so müde.
example.en: I really ought to study, but I am so tired.

cards.more: Sollte is built like a past tense: stem soll + te, then the normal past endings. Ich sollte, du solltest, er sollte. Ich and er look the same, just like ich konnte and er konnte. Now the spelling trap. Könnte gets dots because können is one of the verbs that take an umlaut in the Konjunktiv II (also dürfte, müsste). Sollen never gets dots, in no form at all, and neither does wollen (wollte). So söllte does not exist. If you see dots on soll-, it is always a mistake.

cards.title: The trap: soll, sollte (past), sollte (advice)
cards.body: Sollte has two meanings. In the past it means was supposed to (früher, gestern, als Kind). Today, for advice, it is Konjunktiv II. Soll is different: someone else wants something now. Look at the time word: früher or gestern means past. No past time word, and you are giving a tip: advice.
cards.lead: You now know sollte, but it looks like a form you met in chapter 2. This card shows how to tell the two meanings apart.

examples.de: Der Lehrer sagt, ich soll mehr lesen.
examples.en: The teacher says I should read more.

examples.de: Früher sollte ich jeden Tag Klavier üben.
examples.en: In the past I was supposed to practise the piano every day.
You should practise more.

deeper.text: The trap is biggest with ich: Ich sollte can be past or advice. Ask two questions. Is there a past time word like gestern? Then it is the past. Am I giving someone a tip for today or the future? Then it is advice. Context decides.

example.de: Gestern sollte ich früh schlafen.
example.en: Yesterday I was supposed to sleep early.

cards.more: Picture three people at a table. Soll is the messenger: someone else wants something, and he passes it on now. Sollte in the past is the storyteller: he tells you what you were supposed to do back then, with words like früher or gestern. Sollte for advice is the kind friend: he gives a tip for today or tomorrow. All three look almost the same, so look around the verb. A past time word means the storyteller. No past word and a tip means the friend.

rows: Der Lehrer sagt, ich soll mehr lesen.
Früher sollte ich jeden Tag üben.

cards.title: Nicht in advice: what you should not do
cards.body: You can also advise someone against something. Put nicht before the infinitive at the end: Du solltest das nicht aufschieben. With a short sentence nicht comes right after solltest: Du solltest nicht so spät lernen. Separable verbs stay in one piece at the end: aufschieben, nachschlagen.
cards.lead: Good advice says what to do and what not to do. Here you add nicht to your new sentences, using the rule you know for modal verbs.

examples.de: Du solltest nicht so spät lernen.
examples.en: You should not study so late.
Ben should not put it off.

examples.de: Du solltest das Wort nicht sofort nachschlagen.
examples.en: You should not look the word up immediately.

deeper.text: Nicht goes in front of the word group you deny, so the infinitive often comes right after it. In Mira sollte nicht alles aufschieben, nicht denies the whole action. If you want a softer tip, you can start with lieber (you will meet it in the next lesson). For now you build every negative tip with nicht before the end.

example.de: Mira sollte nicht alles aufschieben.
example.en: Mira should not put everything off.

cards.more: Think of nicht as a small stop sign that you put right in front of the action you want to stop. The action is the infinitive at the end: aufschieben, lernen, nachschlagen. So the order is: person, solltest, the middle part, nicht, infinitive. English puts not after should: you should not put it off. German puts nicht further back, close to the last verb. A quick test: say the sentence and check that the infinitive is the very last word.

rows: Du solltest lernen nicht so spät.
Du solltest nicht so spät lernen.

steps: Du solltest …
… das …
… nicht …
… aufschieben.

cards.title: Ben and Mira: a small advice dialogue
cards.body: Now you hear all the parts together. Ben tells Mira his problem. Mira asks a question, listens and gives two pieces of advice with solltest. Ben reacts and thanks her. Notice how often the infinitive stands at the end of Mira's sentences. Danke für den Tipp! is a fixed phrase: you can learn it as one piece.
cards.lead: You can name a problem and give advice. This last card joins everything into a short real dialogue between Ben and Mira.

examples.en: I cannot concentrate.
When do you study?

examples.de: Immer abends, aber dann bin ich müde.
examples.en: Always in the evening, but then I am tired.
You should study in the morning.
And you should sleep earlier.
Thanks for the tip!

deeper.text: Look at Mira's question: Wann lernst du denn? The little word denn adds no new meaning. It makes a question sound interested and friendly, not like a test. Germans often use it when they ask about a problem. Without denn, Wann lernst du? can sound a bit cold. This little denn belongs to questions, not to advice sentences.

example.de: Was ist denn los, Ben?
example.en: What's the matter, Ben?

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a short play with two actors. Ben brings the problem. Mira first asks a question, because a good friend listens before giving advice. Then she gives two tips, both with solltest and the infinitive at the end. Ben closes with Danke für den Tipp! Now play it again and change the tips yourself: Du solltest das Wort nachschlagen, Du solltest nicht alles aufschieben. Same frame, new tips. That is exactly how real conversations work.
steps: The problem: Ich kann mich nicht konzentrieren.
A question: Wann lernst du denn?
The advice: Du solltest morgens lernen.
The thanks: Danke für den Tipp!

lessons.title: Ihr solltet früher anfangen: all forms, questions, Sie sollten
lessons.goal: Advise one person, a group or a stranger with all forms of sollte, ask for advice with Was sollte ich tun? and say what not to do with kein and nicht.

grammar.topic: all forms of sollte; questions; Sie sollten; kein in advice
grammar.point: Sollte has six forms: ich sollte, du solltest, er/sie/es sollte, wir sollten, ihr solltet, sie/Sie sollten. Polite advice uses Sie sollten. In questions the verb moves: Was sollte ich tun? / Sollte ich …? The infinitive stays at the end. Kein goes with a noun that has no article; nicht goes with the verb.

mistake.why: The ihr form always ends in -t: ihr solltet, like ihr konntet. Only wir and sie/Sie take -n: sollten.

terms.meaning: advice for several friends: the ihr form ends in -t
polite advice to a stranger or adult: same form as sie sollten, written with a capital S
better, rather: Du solltest lieber früh schlafen

cards.title: Before we start: advice for everyone
cards.body: Ben's Klausur is in two weeks. Now not only Mira gives advice: Anna, the whole WG and even Frau Weber have tips. They talk to one person, to several people and sometimes politely. Today you learn all the forms of sollte, how to ask for advice yourself, and how to say what someone should not do.
steps: You already know: Du solltest mehr schlafen, Ben sollte früher anfangen, and Was soll ich machen? (soll, from the present).
New today: wir sollten, ihr solltet, Sie sollten, questions like Was sollte ich tun?, and keinen / keine in advice.
By the end you can: advise one person, a group or a stranger, and ask for advice before an exam.

examples.en: You should sleep more.
examples.why: You know this already: du solltest.

examples.en: What should I do?
examples.why: You know this already: soll in a question.

examples.en: You (all) should start earlier.

cards.more: Imagine the WG kitchen the evening before Ben's exam. Mira talks to Ben alone: du solltest. Then she turns to Ben and Anna together: ihr solltet. Then Frau Weber knocks on the door, and Mira is polite: Sie sollten. Later Ben asks: Was sollte ich tun? Four situations, one idea. The frame never moves: sollte-form in position 2, infinitive at the end. Only the small ending on sollte changes, like a name badge for each person.

cards.title: Die Klausur: words for exam time
cards.body: Ben has a Klausur in two weeks. He needs a Lernplan and a Zeitplan. Anna suggests a Lerngruppe and Karteikarten. Before the exam he has Prüfungsangst: his Aufregung is big, and Mira has Lampenfieber before every talk. Wiederholung is important, and a Notiz helps. Learn these nine words with their articles.
cards.lead: Ben's exam is the topic of this chapter. First you need the vocabulary around it, in short present-tense sentences you can already read.

examples.de: Ben hat in zwei Wochen eine Klausur.
examples.en: Ben has an exam in two weeks.
He makes a study plan.
He has exam anxiety.

deeper.text: Look closely at the joints of long nouns. Prüfung + Angst gets a small s in the middle: Prüfungsangst. Lampe + Fieber gets an n: Lampenfieber. Germans call this a joining sound; it only helps you say the word. Words ending in -ung almost always take that s, as in Zeitungsartikel. The last part still decides the article: die Angst, so die Prüfungsangst.

example.de: Ben hat oft Prüfungsangst.
example.en: Ben often has exam anxiety.

cards.more: Think of exam time as a little film in three scenes. Scene one, planning: der Lernplan, der Zeitplan, die Lerngruppe. Scene two, learning: die Karteikarte, die Notiz, die Wiederholung. Scene three, the day itself: die Klausur, die Aufregung, die Prüfungsangst, and Lampenfieber if you must speak in front of people. Sort the words into the three scenes in your head. Words in a little story stick much better than words in a long list.

rows: Die Klausur ist in zwei Wochen.
Der Zeitplan ist an der Wand.
Ich schreibe das Wort auf eine Karteikarte.
Vor der Klausur ist die Aufregung groß.

cards.title: The full table: ich, du, er, wir, ihr, sie
cards.body: Now all six persons. Ich and er/sie/es are the same: sollte. Du takes -st: solltest. Wir and sie take -n: sollten. Ihr takes -t: solltet. There is no umlaut anywhere. The sentence stays the same: sollte is in position 2, the infinitive stands at the end.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you used ich, du and er. This card completes the table, so you can advise a group and talk about other people.

examples.en: We should look for a study group.
You (all) should start earlier.

examples.de: Ben und Anna sollten mehr üben.
examples.en: Ben and Anna should practise more.

deeper.text: A good way to remember: sollte follows the same pattern as the past of modal verbs. You know konnte and musste: ich konnte, du konntest, wir konnten, ihr konntet. Sollte works exactly the same. If you can form musstet, you can form solltet. Only the meaning is new: advice.

example.de: Ihr solltet nicht so lange warten.
example.en: You should not wait so long.

cards.more: Look at the endings like four little hats. Ich and er wear no hat: sollte. Du wears -st: solltest. Wir and sie wear -n: sollten. Ihr wears -t: solltet. English needs only one form, should, for everybody, so German feels like more work. But you already know these hats from the past of modal verbs: ich konnte, ihr konntet. Say the six forms aloud with a clap on each ending, and ihr solltet will stop sounding strange.

rows: Anna und Ben sollten mehr üben.

cards.title: Polite advice: Sie sollten …
cards.body: To a stranger or an adult you do not know well, use Sie. The verb form is the same as for sie (they): sollten. Write Sie with a capital letter. Frau Weber speaks like this to a neighbour, and a course teacher speaks like this to the whole course. Compare three people in the table.
cards.lead: You can advise friends. But what do you say to a neighbour or a teacher? This card gives you the polite form.

examples.en: You should take a break.
You should practise every day.

examples.de: Herr Ali, Sie sollten mehr Italienisch sprechen.
examples.en: Herr Ali, you should speak more Italian.

deeper.text: For Sie you can add the name first: Herr Ali, Sie sollten … The comma stays after the name. Be careful with the capital: Sie (polite you) and sie (they) both use sollten, but the polite one is always written with S. The context tells you which one is meant.

example.de: Frau Weber, Sie sollten nicht so viel arbeiten.
example.en: Frau Weber, you should not work so much.

cards.more: Think of three doors. The du door is for one friend, a child or family. The ihr door is for a group of friends. The Sie door is for a stranger, a teacher, a neighbour like Frau Weber, a doctor. Behind the Sie door the verb is always sollten, exactly like sie (they). The only difference is the big S. In speech you cannot hear the capital, so the situation tells you who is meant: one adult you address politely, or a group of other people.

cards.title: Asking for advice: Was sollte ich tun?
cards.body: You can ask for advice with sollte, too. In a W-question the question word comes first and sollte is in position 2: Was sollte ich tun? In a yes/no question sollte is first: Sollte ich eine Lerngruppe suchen? The infinitive is still at the end. Answer: Ja, das solltest du. or Nein, du solltest lieber …
cards.lead: Now turn it around: you ask for advice. The question uses the same pieces, but sollte moves to the front.

examples.en: What should I do?
When should I start?
How much should I study?
Should I look for a study group?

deeper.text: The answer to a yes/no question can be short. Ja, das solltest du. means: yes, you should do that. Notice that the person changes: you ask about ich, but the answer is about du. To say no politely, use lieber: Nein, du solltest lieber allein lernen. The word lieber means better, rather.

example.de: Ja, das solltest du.
example.en: Yes, you should do that.

cards.more: A question is the same sentence with the furniture moved. Statement: Ich sollte eine Lerngruppe suchen. Yes/no question: Sollte ich eine Lerngruppe suchen? The verb jumps to the front. With a question word, the word takes the first seat and the verb sits in seat two: Was sollte ich tun? Wann sollte ich anfangen? In every version, the infinitive stays on the last chair. English does the same jump: I should go becomes Should I go?
steps: Question word (or nothing for yes/no)
sollte / sollten
The subject: ich, wir, …
The rest, then the infinitive at the end

cards.title: Keinen Kaffee, keine Angst: kein in advice
cards.body: You know kein for nouns without an article and nicht for verbs. They work in advice, too. Use kein when the noun has no article: Du solltest keinen Kaffee mehr trinken. Use nicht when you deny the action or the noun has the article: Du solltest die Karteikarten nicht vergessen. Kein gets the ending you know.
cards.lead: Advice often says what to leave out. You know kein from A1; here it joins your advice sentences.

examples.de: Du solltest keinen Kaffee mehr trinken.
examples.en: You should not drink coffee any more.
You should not be afraid.

examples.de: Du solltest die Karteikarten nicht vergessen.
examples.en: You should not forget the flashcards.

deeper.text: If you are unsure, ask: is there a noun without an article, like Kaffee or Angst? Then kein. Is there already a definite article, die Karteikarten, or only an action? Then nicht. Kein follows the same endings as ein: keinen for a masculine noun in the accusative, keine for feminine and plural.

example.de: Ben sollte nicht so lange warten.
example.en: Ben should not wait so long.

cards.more: Use a quick test from English. If you would say no coffee or not a coffee, German uses kein: keinen Kaffee, keine Angst. If you would say not plus a verb, or the noun already has the, German uses nicht: nicht warten, die Karteikarten nicht vergessen. So kein sits right in front of a noun like a little lid. Nicht stands before the action at the end. And kein takes the same endings as ein: keinen for der-words in the accusative.

rows: a noun with ein or no article
Du solltest die Karte nicht vergessen.

cards.title: Lieber and a small dialogue: Ben and Anna
cards.body: Lieber (better, rather) makes advice more specific: Du solltest lieber früh schlafen. It says: this is the better choice. Now read how Ben asks Anna for advice about his Prüfungsangst. Notice the three kinds of sentences: a statement, questions with sollte and advice with solltest. Viel Erfolg! means good luck.
cards.lead: You can ask, advise and say what not to do. This last card puts everything together in a short dialogue between Ben and Anna.

examples.en: I have exam anxiety.
What should I do?
You had better go to bed early.
Should I look for a study group?
Yes, you should.
Don't worry! Good luck!

deeper.text: Lieber is not a new word; it is the comparative of gern. You know Ich trinke gern Tee. Ich trinke lieber Tee means: I prefer tea. In advice, lieber carries that same idea of a better choice: Du solltest lieber schlafen says sleep instead of what you are doing now. So lieber always hides a comparison, even when the other option is not said.

lessons.title: Ich finde, du solltest …: advice in side sentences and how strong it is
lessons.goal: Give and react to advice in longer sentences: sollte at the end of dass, wenn and ob sentences, the strength of musst, solltest, könntest and kannst, and reactions to a tip.

grammar.topic: sollte in side sentences; strength of advice; reacting
grammar.point: In dass, weil and ob sentences the verbs go to the end, and sollte takes the very last place: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest. After a wenn sentence at the front, the main part starts with the verb: Wenn du müde bist, solltest du eine Pause machen. Musst is a rule, solltest good advice, könntest an idea, kannst a possibility.
grammar.oneLine: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest.

mistake.wrong: Ich finde, dass du solltest mehr üben.
mistake.right: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest.
mistake.why: In a side sentence the finite verb goes to the very end. Sollte stands last, after the infinitive.

terms.meaning: after dass, weil, ob: the infinitive first, then sollte at the very end
memory trick: a bridge for your memory
Du musst (rule) > Du solltest (advice) > Du könntest (idea) > Du kannst (possible)

cards.title: Before we start: advice inside a longer sentence
cards.body: Ben has a Lernplan idea, but advice does not always come in short sentences. People say: Ich finde, dass du … or Wenn du müde bist, solltest du … Also, advice can be strong or weak, like a traffic light. And when you get a tip, you want to react. Today you learn all three.
steps: You already know: Du solltest mehr üben, Ihr solltet früher anfangen, and side sentences with dass, wenn and ob (the verb goes to the end).
New today: sollte at the end of a side sentence, the strength of advice (musst, solltest, könntest, kannst), and how to react to a tip.
By the end you can: give advice in a longer sentence, choose how strong it is, and answer when someone gives you a tip.

cards.more: Picture three tools in a box. Tool one: a longer sentence. Instead of a short Du solltest mehr üben, you say Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest. It sounds more personal, like your own opinion. Tool two: a strength dial, from Du musst (a rule) down to Du kannst (just possible). Tool three: answers to a tip, like Gute Idee! The good news: the side-sentence rule is old. Dass sends the verb to the end, as always.

cards.title: Wörter für das Lernen: methods and habits
cards.body: Everyone learns differently. Which Lerntyp are you? Anna uses a Methode with music, Ben tries a new Lernstrategie. A good Gewohnheit brings Fortschritt and Lernerfolg. A Belohnung after learning feels good. For hard words an Eselsbrücke helps. Try things out (ausprobieren) and learn the important words auswendig.
cards.lead: Before the grammar, here are the ten words about how people learn and what helps. Read them in simple sentences first.

examples.en: Ben tries out the method.

deeper.text: Auswendig originally meant from the outside: you can say the text without looking into the book. It goes with two verbs. Ich lerne die Wörter auswendig describes the work. Ich kann die Wörter auswendig describes the result: I know them by heart. Eselsbrücke literally means donkey bridge: a little bridge that gets a stubborn donkey across a stream, and gets your memory across a hard word.

example.de: Mira kann den Text auswendig.
example.en: Mira knows the text by heart.

cards.more: Think of learning like cooking. Everybody has a different kitchen: that is your Lerntyp. The recipe you follow is the Methode or Lernstrategie. Doing it every day turns it into a Gewohnheit. Then you taste the result: Fortschritt, and in the end Lernerfolg. Dessert is the Belohnung. An Eselsbrücke is a little kitchen trick that saves time. Ausprobieren means trying a new recipe for a week. Auswendig means you can cook it without the book.

rows: Eine Pause ist eine gute Gewohnheit.
Nach dem Lernen gibt es eine Belohnung.

cards.title: Ich finde, dass du … solltest: sollte at the end
cards.body: In a dass sentence the verbs go to the end, and sollte takes the very last place: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest. First comes the infinitive (üben), then sollte. Use it after Ich finde, Ich glaube or Anna meint. Colours as in chapter 5: sollte is the Konjunktiv II colour, the infinitive stays in the second-verb colour.
cards.lead: You know how a dass sentence puts the verb at the end. Here you add sollte: two verbs at the end, in a fixed order.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest.
examples.en: I think you should practise more.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Ben eine Pause machen sollte.
examples.en: I think Ben should take a break.

examples.de: Anna meint, dass wir eine Lerngruppe suchen sollten.
examples.en: Anna thinks we should look for a study group.

deeper.text: In everyday speech, many Germans leave out dass after Ich finde and Ich glaube. Then the second part keeps normal main-sentence order: Ich finde, du solltest mehr üben. Both versions are correct. With dass the verb goes to the end; without dass it stays in position 2. Never mix the two: Ich finde, dass du solltest mehr üben is wrong.

example.de: Ich finde, du solltest früher anfangen.
example.en: I think you should start earlier.

cards.more: Think of a train where the engine is at the back. In a normal sentence the engine, solltest, is the second carriage. After dass, the whole verb group rolls to the end and the engine goes last: dass du mehr üben solltest. English keeps should in the middle: that you should practise more. German waits. A simple method: build the short sentence first, Du solltest mehr üben. Then add Ich finde, dass, and push solltest behind üben.

rows: Ich finde, dass du mehr üben solltest.
Ich glaube, dass Ben eine Pause machen sollte.

steps: Main sentence: Du solltest mehr üben.
Add the frame: Ich finde, dass …
dass + du + mehr: the subject follows dass
Verbs at the end: … üben solltest.

cards.title: Wenn du müde bist, solltest du …: wenn and ob
cards.body: Sollte also works in wenn and ob sentences. In a wenn sentence at the front, the second part starts with the verb: Wenn du müde bist, solltest du eine Pause machen. In an ob sentence sollte is last: Ben weiß nicht, ob er eine Lerngruppe suchen sollte. This works exactly like the sentences you know from chapter 7.
cards.lead: Two more side-sentence frames. With wenn you give a condition for the advice; with ob you pass on a question.

examples.de: Wenn du müde bist, solltest du eine Pause machen.
examples.en: If you are tired, you should take a break.

examples.de: Wenn du Prüfungsangst hast, solltest du eine Lerngruppe suchen.
examples.en: If you have exam anxiety, you should look for a study group.

examples.de: Ben weiß nicht, ob er eine Lerngruppe suchen sollte.
examples.en: Ben does not know whether he should look for a study group.

deeper.text: English uses if for two different German words. When you mean in case or whenever, use wenn: Wenn du müde bist, … When you mean whether, a hidden yes/no question, use ob: Ich weiß nicht, ob … A quick test: if you can say whether in English, German needs ob. Both send the verbs to the end of their part of the sentence.

example.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob ich heute lernen sollte.
example.en: I don't know whether I should study today.

cards.more: With wenn at the front, the sentence has two parts. Part 1 is the wenn sentence with its verb at the end. Part 2 starts with the verb: solltest du. Think of the wenn part as one block that stands in position 1. For ob you need a question in the sentence: Sollte ich eine Lerngruppe suchen? becomes Ich weiß nicht, ob ich eine Lerngruppe suchen sollte.

cards.title: Muss, sollte, könnte, kann: how strong is it?
cards.body: The four verbs give four strengths. Du musst is a rule: you have no choice. Du solltest is good advice. Du könntest is an idea. Du kannst says it is possible. The imperative is direct: Mach eine Pause! Choose the verb that fits what you want to say. Advice with solltest is not an order.
cards.lead: Same sentence, four verbs, four strengths. You know all four verbs already, now compare them.

examples.en: You must take a break.
You should take a break.
You could take a break.
You can take a break.

deeper.text: Choosing the right strength is polite. With a friend you can say Du solltest. With a teacher or a stranger you often use Sie könnten or Sie sollten. The direct form, the imperative, is the strongest and most personal: Mach eine Pause! You say it to a friend who really needs it. Be careful with Du musst: it sounds like an order.

example.de: Mach eine Pause!
example.en: Take a break!

cards.more: Think of a traffic light with an extra light. Du musst is red: a rule, no choice, like Du musst pünktlich kommen. Du solltest is orange: wise advice. Du könntest is a soft green: just an idea you can take or leave. Du kannst is plain green: you are allowed, it is possible. In English it is the same ladder: must, should, could, can. Most of the time, a friend giving advice stays on orange or soft green.
steps: Du musst … = rule, no choice
Du solltest … = good advice
Du könntest … = an idea
Du kannst … = it is possible

cards.title: Gute Idee! Reacting to advice
cards.body: When someone gives you a tip, you answer. You can like it (Gute Idee!), promise to try it (Das probiere ich aus.), say you already tried it (Das habe ich schon probiert, aber …), thank the person (Danke, das mache ich.) or be unsure (Hm, ich weiß nicht.). Choose the reaction that is true for you.
cards.lead: A tip is only half of a conversation. The other half is your answer: you can like it, try it, refuse it politely or ask for more.

examples.en: Good idea!
I will try that out.

examples.de: Das habe ich schon probiert, aber es hat nicht geholfen.
examples.en: I have tried that already, but it did not help.

deeper.text: Notice the small word aber: Das habe ich schon probiert, aber … is polite because you first say you tried, and then you give your problem. Ausprobieren is separable: Das probiere ich aus. In the Perfekt it is one word: Das habe ich ausprobiert. After the reaction you can ask for another tip: Hast du noch einen Tipp?

example.de: Hast du noch einen Tipp?
example.en: Do you have another tip?

cards.more: Imagine a menu in a café: you choose the reaction that fits your feeling. Like the tip? Gute Idee! Want to test it? Das probiere ich aus. Already tried it? Das habe ich schon probiert, aber es hat nicht geholfen. Will follow it? Danke, das mache ich. Not convinced? Hm, ich weiß nicht. In English you would also never stay silent after a tip. Learn two of these by heart today, and you can survive every advice conversation.

rows: Das habe ich schon probiert, aber …

cards.title: Mein Tipp: other ways to give advice, and a dialogue
cards.body: You can also start advice with a frame: Mein Tipp: Mach einen Lernplan! Or: Es ist wichtig, dass du jeden Tag lernst. Or: Am besten lernst du morgens. Read the dialogue: Mira, Anna and Leon help Ben, and he finally makes a Lernplan. Look for the frames, the sollte sentence and Ben's reactions.
cards.lead: You know sollte and its reactions. This last card adds three more advice frames and puts everything together in a short chat.

examples.de: Gute Idee! Das probiere ich aus.

deeper.text: Am besten is the top step of gut, besser, am besten. So Am besten lernst du morgens literally says: you learn best in the morning. People often use it instead of sollte, because it sounds like shared experience, not a lecture. Am besten takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject follows it.

example.de: Am besten fragst du Frau Weber.
example.en: It's best to ask Frau Weber.

cards.more: Good advice is like a good meal: not every dish has the same taste. If you say Du solltest five times, it sounds like a list from a teacher. So mix frames. Mein Tipp: Mach einen Lernplan! is short and direct. Es ist wichtig, dass du jeden Tag lernst sounds serious. Am besten lernst du morgens sounds like experience. Read the dialogue and find each frame. Then write three tips for Ben, each with a different frame.

lessons.title: Was für ein Kurs ist das? Asking about the kind of thing
lessons.goal: Ask what kind of course, book or teacher it is with Was für ein / eine / einen …? and answer with ein + adjective.

grammar.topic: Was für ein …? in the nominative and accusative
grammar.point: Was für ein/eine/ein …? asks for the kind of something. Ein matches the noun, and its case comes from the verb, not from für: Was für ein Kurs ist das? (nominative after ist), Was für einen Kurs machst du? (accusative after machen). Answers use ein + adjective + noun with the endings from A2 chapter 6. Welcher? asks for one thing from a list. Plural and uncountable nouns have no ein: Was für Bücher liest du? – Krimis.

mistake.why: The case comes from the verb, not from für. After ist the noun is the subject, so it is nominative: ein Kurs. Only after a verb like machen do you say einen Kurs.

terms.meaning: what kind of …? (asks for the sort of thing)

Today you open the piece and look inside: where ein comes from, why it sometimes becomes einen, and how to answer. Go step by step. Every card adds one small thing.

cards.body: Anna wants to learn Italian. Many towns have a Volkshochschule, an adult education centre with evening courses. Die Fortgeschrittenen are learners with more experience.

deeper.text: Many words come as a pair: der Kursleiter is a man, die Kursleiterin a woman, and die Kursleiter means several men or a mixed group. Use die Fortgeschrittenen only as a whole piece, and in the chunk für Fortgeschrittene. Das Niveau (the level) comes from French, its plural is die Niveaus. These pair words are very common in German courses.

example.de: Der Kurs für Fortgeschrittene ist am Dienstag.
example.en: The course for advanced learners is on Tuesday.

cards.more: Picture the Volkshochschule as a big school building for grown-ups. Inside, each room has a sign. Der Sprachkurs is the lesson itself. Der Kursleiter or die Kursleiterin stands at the front. The Teilnehmer sit at the tables, and every Anfänger starts with an Einstufungstest, a little quiz that shows the right Niveau. The Lehrbuch is the book, and the Lernplattform is the same book on a screen. Learn each word with its der, die or das.

cards.title: Was für ein …? asks what kind
cards.body: Was für ein …? means what kind of …? You ask it when you want to know the sort of thing, not which single one. Build it in five steps. Ein matches the noun: ein Kurs, eine Kursleiterin, ein Lehrbuch. Here the noun is the subject of ist, so it is in the nominative.
cards.lead: Now you know the words. On this card you learn the question itself: Was für ein …? and the five steps that build it, so you can ask what kind of course, teacher or book you have.

examples.de: Was für ein Kurs ist das?
examples.en: What kind of course is that?

examples.de: Was für eine Kursleiterin ist das?
examples.en: What kind of course teacher is that?

examples.de: Was für ein Lehrbuch ist das?
examples.en: What kind of textbook is that?

deeper.text: Was für ein usually stays together. Especially in speech, Germans also split it: Was ist das für ein Kurs? Was für moves to the front, the verb comes second, and für ein + noun goes behind das. Both versions mean the same and both are correct. You will hear the split one in every course office, so learn to recognise it now.

example.de: Was ist das für ein Kurs?
example.en: What kind of course is that?

cards.more: Imagine you walk into a shop and ask: what sort of bread is that? In English you start with what sort of. German starts with Was für. Then you pick ein, eine or ein to fit the noun, like you always do with a noun: ein Kurs, eine Kursleiterin, ein Lehrbuch. Then the verb, then the rest. Say it five times with five nouns and the pattern sits in your head. Start with Was für. Add the little word. Add the noun.

rows: Was für ein Kurs ist das?
Was für eine Kursleiterin ist das?
Was für ein Lehrbuch ist das?

steps: Was für: start with these two words
ein, eine or ein: it matches the noun
the noun: Kurs, Kursleiterin, Lehrbuch
the verb: ist
the rest: das?

cards.title: Important: für does not decide the case
cards.body: Many learners think für means accusative and say Was für einen Kurs ist das? That is wrong. The case comes from the verb, as always. After ist the noun is the subject: ein Kurs. After machen it is the object: einen Kurs. Only the der-words change. Eine Kursleiterin and ein Lehrbuch stay the same.
cards.lead: You can build the question. Now comes the trap: the little word für looks as if it should change ein. This card shows what really decides the ending, so you get ein and einen right.

examples.de: Was für einen Kurs machst du?
examples.en: What kind of course are you doing?

examples.de: Was für eine Kursleiterin suchst du?
examples.en: What kind of course teacher are you looking for?
examples.why: die-word: eine, same in both cases.

examples.de: Was für ein Lehrbuch brauchst du?
examples.en: What kind of textbook do you need?

deeper.text: Ask who does something. In Was für ein Kurs ist das? nobody does anything to the Kurs: it just is. In Was für einen Kurs machst du? you do something to the Kurs. After ist the noun is nominative. After machen, suchen, brauchen and haben it is accusative. You already know this rule from A1: the verb tells you the case.

example.de: Was für einen Lehrer hast du?
example.en: What kind of teacher do you have?

cards.more: Do a quick check. Look at the verb before the noun. Is it ist? Then use ein. Is it machen, suchen, brauchen or haben? Then use einen for a der-word. For die-words and das-words nothing changes, so you cannot make a mistake with eine and ein. A trap to remember: Was für ein Lehrbuch brauchst du? is fine, because ein is also the accusative of the das-word. But Was für ein Kurs machst du? is wrong. Say einen Kurs.

Was für einen Kurs machst du?

Was für ein Lehrbuch brauchst du?

cards.title: Answering: ein + adjective + noun
cards.body: Answer with ein, eine or einen, an adjective and the noun. You know the endings from A2 chapter 6. The answer has the case of the question: nominative after ist, accusative after machen. Only the der-words change: ein kleiner Kurs (nominative), einen kleinen Kurs (accusative).
cards.lead: You can ask the question. Now the answer: this card puts the adjective endings from chapter 6 to work. It is the same ein + adjective chain you used for Job, now with course, teacher and book.

examples.en: A small course.
examples.why: Answer to Was für ein Kurs ist das?

examples.en: A small course.
examples.why: Answer to Was für einen Kurs machst du?

deeper.text: A full answer often starts with Das ist: Das ist ein dickes Lehrbuch. In a short answer you drop it. The ending always sits on the adjective, not on ein: einen kleinen Kurs, but ein dickes Lehrbuch. The ending -es for the das-word is the same in the nominative and the accusative, so for das-words you have only one form to learn.

example.de: Das ist ein dickes Lehrbuch.
example.en: That is a thick textbook.

cards.more: It is like a little sandwich. The question is the top bread. The answer is the filling with three layers: ein-word, adjective, noun. When the question has einen, copy einen into the answer and give the adjective an -en. When the question has ein for a der-word, the answer gets ein and the adjective gets -er. Take an easy adjective like klein, nett or neu and practise with course, teacher and book. Say each answer aloud.

cards.title: welcher or was für ein?
cards.body: Welcher? asks for one thing out of a group you can see or list. Was für ein? asks for the kind. Test: can you point at a list or a timetable? Then use welcher. Welcher Kurs? The Italian course on Monday. Was für ein Kurs? An evening course for beginners.
cards.lead: You know welcher from A1 and Was für ein from this lesson. Both ask about a noun, but they ask different things. This card gives you a quick test to pick the right one.

examples.en: Which course is that?
examples.why: From a list. Answer: Der Italienischkurs am Montag.

examples.en: What kind of course is that?
examples.why: The kind. Answer: Ein Abendkurs für Anfänger.

examples.en: Which textbook is new?
examples.why: From a list. Answer: Das blaue Lehrbuch.

deeper.text: Welcher has endings that copy der, die, das: welcher Kurs, welche Kursleiterin, welches Lehrbuch. Was für ein keeps Was für and only ein changes. A good habit: if the answer starts with der, die or das, the question was welcher. If the answer starts with ein or eine, the question was was für ein. Check the first word of the answer and you know.

example.de: Welcher Lehrer ist neu?
example.en: Which teacher is new?

cards.more: Imagine a bakery. You point at the glass and say: that one, please. That is welcher: you choose from what is in front of you. Now imagine you have never seen the bakery and ask: what sort of bread do you have? That is was für ein: you want to learn the kind. At a course desk there are often both: first you ask what kind of course it is, then you choose which one on the list. Welcher stays in the list. Was für ein goes to the label.

rows: Was für ein Kurs ist das?

cards.title: Plural and words without a plural
cards.body: With plural nouns and with words that have no plural you cannot use ein. Say Was für Bücher …? or Was für Musik …? with no article. Answer with the bare noun: Krimis. or Jazz. Keep it short. This is a very common small-talk question about taste.
cards.lead: So far you asked about one course, one teacher, one book. Now you ask about many things or about a whole topic like music, and see that ein simply disappears. This card ends the lesson with a conversation at the course desk.

examples.en: What kind of books do you read?
What kind of music do you listen to?

examples.de: Was für Kurse gibt es hier?
examples.en: What kind of courses are there here?

deeper.text: Was für ein also works as an exclamation, with no question at all: Was für ein Tag! means What a day! Germans say it when something is very good or very bad, and the voice goes down at the end, not up. The adjective endings stay the same as in the answers you practised: ein schöner Tag, eine tolle Idee.

example.de: Was für ein schöner Tag!
example.en: What a beautiful day!

cards.more: In English you say what kind of books, with no a. German does the same: Was für Bücher. There is nothing to match, so there is no ein to pick and no ending to get wrong. That is why this card is the easiest one. Think of it as the easy mode of the question. Use it for things you like, such as books, films or music, and for the topic of a whole course. Read the little dialogue aloud twice and listen to the rhythm.

lessons.title: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du? Talking about work
lessons.goal: Ask and answer about where and how people work with Was für in the nominative, accusative and dative, and give short advice at work.

grammar.topic: Was für with a preposition + dative
grammar.point: After in, bei or mit (wo?, with arbeiten) the noun is dative, so ein becomes einem (der-word, das-word) or einer (die-word): In was für einer Firma arbeitest du? Mit was für einem Team? Answers use einem/einer + adjective with -en: In einer kleinen Firma. Mit einem jungen Team. Without a preposition the case follows the verb as in lesson 4.
grammar.oneLine: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du? In einer kleinen Firma.

mistake.wrong: In was für ein Firma arbeitest du?
mistake.right: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
mistake.why: After in with wo? the noun is dative. Firma is a die-word, so ein becomes einer.

terms.meaning: what kind of … (dative, after a preposition)
the case after in, bei, mit (wo?): einem for der- and das-words, einer for die-words
boss: learn meine Vorgesetzte / mein Vorgesetzter

cards.title: Before we start: the preposition comes first
cards.body: Mira works bei einer großen Firma, and Anna asks about it. At work you often ask about a place or a team, and then a preposition leads the question: in, bei, mit. Today Was für gets its dative form, so you can ask In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
steps: You already know: Was für einen Kurs machst du? from lesson 4, and bei einer großen Firma with the dative -en ending from A2 chapter 6.
New today: a preposition in front of Was für, then einem or einer: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
By the end you can: ask and answer about your company, your team and your work, and give advice about work.

examples.de: Ich arbeite bei einer großen Firma.
examples.en: I work for a large company.

examples.de: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
examples.en: In what kind of company do you work?
examples.why: New today: preposition first, then was für einer.

examples.en: In a small company.
examples.why: New today: the short answer after the question.

cards.more: Remember the sandwich from lesson 4: Was für ein is the top bread. Today a small piece of bread goes on top of the top bread: a preposition. Mira says In was für einer Firma. The little word in belongs to the place (in einer Firma), so the whole group stands first, and then everything else follows as usual. Nothing in lesson 4 was wrong. You only add one more word at the start and change ein into einer or einem, the dative. Take it slowly, card by card.

cards.title: Arbeitsalltag: ten words about work
cards.body: Ten words help you talk about work. Die Branche is the sector, for example die Gastronomie. Der Arbeitsalltag is your normal working day, die Tätigkeit what you do. Der Dienstplan shows who works when, das Betriebsklima is the mood at work, die Weiterbildung is further training. Der Küchenchef leads the kitchen.
cards.lead: In lesson 4 the words were about courses. Now you need words for the workplace, so that your questions and answers have real content: ten nouns about sectors, tasks, rosters and bosses.

examples.en: The head chef makes the duty roster.

examples.de: Das Betriebsklima im Team ist gut.
examples.en: The working atmosphere in the team is good.
Mira is doing further training.

deeper.text: Der Arbeitsalltag has no plural: it means the normal day in general. Das Kollegium is all the colleagues together, like the staff of a school; the plural is die Kollegien. For the boss, learn two forms for now: meine Vorgesetzte for a woman and mein Vorgesetzter for a man. Use only these two forms; other forms follow later.

example.de: Meine Vorgesetzte ist sehr nett.
example.en: My boss is very nice.

cards.more: Imagine one day at work as a small film. The Branche is the genre, for example Gastronomie. The Tätigkeit is your role in the film. The Dienstplan is the schedule that says when you are on screen. The Betriebsklima is the mood in the room, good or bad. At the end you may decide to do a Weiterbildung to get a bigger role. Say each word with its article. For Vorgesetzte, learn only meine Vorgesetzte and mein Vorgesetzter.

cards.title: Preposition + was für + dative
cards.body: A question about a place or a team often starts with a preposition: in, bei, mit. After it comes was für and then ein in the dative: einem for der-words and das-words, einer for die-words. You know in, bei and mit with the dative from A1. In was für einer Firma arbeitest du? The question still asks for the kind.
cards.lead: In lesson 4 the question started the sentence. This card moves a preposition in front and shows that the dative of ein changes to einem and einer, so you can ask about work places and teams.

examples.de: In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
examples.en: In what kind of company do you work?

examples.de: Mit was für einem Chef arbeitest du?
examples.en: With what kind of boss do you work?

examples.de: In was für einem Team arbeitet Mira?
examples.en: In what kind of team does Mira work?

deeper.text: Work questions with arbeiten are wo? questions: you are in the company, not on the way to it. After in with wo? you always use the dative. If you move to a place, wohin? takes the accusative, but that is a different question. So in, bei and mit with arbeiten are dative friends. The same rule works for other verbs like wohnen: In was für einer Gegend wohnst du?

example.de: In was für einer Gegend wohnst du?
example.en: In what kind of area do you live?

cards.more: Think of three small bags: one for der-words, one for die-words, one for das-words. In the dative, der and das share the bag einem, and die has its own bag einer. When you hear in, bei or mit, open the dative bags: Mit einem Chef. In einer Firma. In einem Team. The question starts with the preposition because the preposition and its noun are one group, and the whole group moves to the front, like in English: In what kind of company do you work? Same order, same idea.

rows: Mit was für einem Chef arbeitest du?
In was für einer Firma arbeitest du?
In was für einem Team arbeitest du?

steps: the preposition: in, bei or mit
Was für: the same two words as before
einem or einer: dative, it matches the noun
the noun: Firma, Team, Chef
the verb and the subject: arbeitest du?

cards.title: Answers in the dative: einem or einer + -en
cards.body: Answer with the same preposition, then einem or einer, an adjective with the ending -en and the noun. In einer kleinen Firma. Mit einem jungen Team. Bei einem großen Betrieb. After einem and einer the adjective always ends in -en, as you learned in A2 chapter 6.
cards.lead: You can ask the question. Now the answer: this card puts the dative of ein and the adjective ending -en together, so you can say what kind of firm, team or boss you have.

examples.en: In a small company.
With a young team.
At a big company.

deeper.text: In a full answer the verb comes second: Ich arbeite in einer kleinen Firma. The short answer starts with the preposition, which is fine because it is only a piece of a sentence. Notice where the endings sit: -em and -er sit on the little word ein, and the adjective always gets -en. Two endings, two jobs, no confusion.

example.de: Ich arbeite in einer kleinen Firma.
example.en: I work in a small company.

cards.more: After einem or einer there is only one adjective ending, and it is the easiest one: -en. So for the answer you need two moves. First pick einem or einer to match the noun. Then add -en to the adjective. Klein becomes kleinen, jung becomes jungen, groß becomes großen. Say In einer kleinen Firma three times, then Mit einem jungen Team. A mistake to avoid: mit einem jung Team. Always add the -en: mit einem jungen Team.

cards.title: The whole Was-für table
cards.body: Here is everything in one table. In the nominative and accusative only the der-word changes: ein Kurs, einen Kurs. In the dative the die-word gets einer, while der-words and das-words both get einem. Plural nouns never take ein. The dative row almost always comes with a preposition, such as in, bei or mit.
cards.lead: You now know three cases of Was für. This card is a summary: it puts nominative, accusative and dative into one table so you can see the pattern and check yourself.

examples.de: Was für ein Chef ist Herr Ali?
examples.en: What kind of boss is Herr Ali?

examples.de: Was für eine Weiterbildung machst du?
examples.en: What kind of further training are you doing?

examples.de: Bei was für einem Betrieb arbeitest du?
examples.en: At what kind of company do you work?

deeper.text: In the plural there is no ein, so the question is just was für + noun: Mit was für Kollegen arbeitest du? The dative plural still leaves a trace: the noun usually gets an extra -n if it does not already end in -n, as in mit Kindern, mit Freunden. Kollegen already ends in -n, so nothing changes there. (Plurals in -s, like mit Autos, stay as they are.) Answer the same way: Mit netten Kollegen.

example.de: Mit was für Kollegen arbeitest du?
example.en: What kind of colleagues do you work with?

cards.more: Look at the table like a small map. Go down the column of a noun and you see how its ein-word changes from case to case. Go across a row and you see what stays the same in one case. The die-word column is the easiest: eine, eine, einer. The das-word column is the sleepy one: ein, ein, einem. The der-word column is the busy one: ein, einen, einem. Walk through the table once with the nouns Kurs, Firma and Team.

cards.title: Talking about your work
cards.body: Use a few set sentences to talk about your work. Ich arbeite in der Gastronomie. Ich arbeite bei einer großen Firma. Mein Arbeitsalltag ist abwechslungsreich. Ich arbeite oft am Abend. Read the two short profiles in the table, then say your own work in three sentences.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer about firms and teams. This card lets you use the work words from the first card in short profiles, so you can introduce your own job to someone at the Volkshochschule.

examples.en: Leon works in the restaurant trade.

examples.de: Mira arbeitet bei einer großen Firma.
examples.en: Mira works for a large company.
Leon often works in the evening.

deeper.text: In a sector you say in der Gastronomie, in a building im Büro, in a firm bei einer Firma. All three are wo? answers, so all three use the dative. You know this pattern from the last card. Mein Arbeitsalltag ist abwechslungsreich is a very good sentence for a profile: it says that every day is different. You can use it for any job.

example.de: Mein Arbeitsalltag ist abwechslungsreich.
example.en: My working day is varied.

cards.more: A profile is a mini story with three sentences: where you work, what your day is like, and when you work. For Leon the story is: Gastronomie, abwechslungsreich, am Abend. For Mira: große Firma, nettes Team, gutes Betriebsklima. Take your own life and fill in the same three boxes. You do not need long sentences. Short and correct beats long and wrong. Read the profiles aloud, then change one word and read them again.

rows: Ich arbeite in der Gastronomie, im Restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Mein Arbeitsalltag ist abwechslungsreich. Ich arbeite oft am Abend.
Ich arbeite bei einer großen Firma. Ich arbeite mit einem netten Team. Das Betriebsklima ist gut.

cards.title: Advice at work
cards.body: Now join the work questions with the advice from lessons 1 to 3. When a friend wants more from work, ask what kind of job it is and give advice with sollte: Du solltest eine Weiterbildung machen. The advice form comes second, the infinitive goes to the end.
cards.lead: This last card combines both parts of the chapter so far: advice with sollte from lessons 1 to 3 and the Was für questions from lessons 4 and 5. Mira and Leon talk about work in a short dialogue.

examples.en: You should do further training.
examples.why: Advice: sollte + infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Du solltest mit dem Küchenchef sprechen.
examples.en: You should talk to the head chef.

examples.de: Was für eine Weiterbildung möchtest du machen?

deeper.text: You can also give advice with Am besten, as in lesson 3: Am besten machst du eine Weiterbildung. After Am besten the verb comes second, like after any first piece. cards.more: Advice is like a small gift. You give it with sollte and you wrap it with a friendly tone. Mira does exactly this for Leon. lessons.title: Ein Interview mit Herrn Ali: report on a working life
lessons.goal: Ask and answer interview questions about a working life, open an interview politely, answer about the past with vor and seit, and report what was said with dass and ob.

grammar.topic: Interview questions, answers in the Perfekt, reporting
grammar.point: An interview mixes W-questions, yes/no questions, Was für ein …? and polite indirect questions (Können Sie uns sagen, wie lange Sie Koch sind?). Answers about the past use the Perfekt and vor/seit + dative; after a time phrase the verb stays in second place: Seit 2010 habe ich ein Restaurant. Report with the Perfekt and a side clause: Herr Ali hat erzählt, dass … Leon hat gefragt, ob …
grammar.oneLine: Können Sie uns sagen, wann Sie angefangen haben? Vor 25 Jahren habe ich angefangen.

mistake.why: The verb is always in second place. If a time phrase is in first place, the verb comes next and the subject after it.

terms.meaning: a polite question inside Können Sie uns sagen, …: the verb goes to the end
vor + dative: an event that is over; seit + dative: still true today
telling what was said: hat erzählt, dass …; hat gefragt, ob …

cards.title: Before we start: an interview for the club newsletter
cards.body: Leon writes for the newsletter of the club „Viertel hilft“. This week he interviews Herr Ali about his life as a cook. A good interview needs polite openings, different kinds of questions and answers about the past. You already know the pieces. Today they work together.
steps: You already know: Seit wann …? from A1 chapter 8, vor + dative from A2 chapter 2, indirect questions with Können Sie mir sagen, … from chapter 7, and Was für ein … from lessons 4 and 5.
New today: a whole interview: opening it, mixing four kinds of questions, answering about the past and reporting what was said.
By the end you can: ask and answer interview questions about a working life, and tell someone what was said.

examples.why: New today: the answer in the Perfekt.

cards.more: Think of an interview as a small ball game. The interviewer throws a question, the guest catches it and throws an answer back. To keep the game going you need different kinds of throws: short ones (yes or no), long ones (when, where, how) and polite ones (Können Sie uns sagen, …). The answers are throws about the past. Nothing here is new grammar. You are only putting the tools from earlier lessons into one conversation. That is real life German.

cards.title: Interviewwörter: ten words for a conversation about work
cards.body: Ten words help you talk about a working life. Das Interview is a planned conversation with questions. Herr Ali is the Interviewpartner. Der Werdegang is the path of a career, das Berufsleben the whole working life. Die Stärke, die Schwäche and die Herausforderung are typical interview topics. Der Berufsanfänger is new in a job.
cards.lead: You know the question patterns and now you need the vocabulary around them: ten nouns for interviews and careers, so your questions and answers have something to talk about.

examples.de: Leon macht ein Interview für „Viertel hilft“.
examples.en: Leon is doing an interview for „Viertel hilft“.

examples.en: Herr Ali is the interviewee today.

examples.en: A career starter often has many questions.

deeper.text: Das Interview comes from English, and its plural is die Interviews. Stärke and Schwäche are die-words with -n in the plural: die Stärken, die Schwächen. Im Rückblick is a handy chunk at the end of an interview: it means looking back. Arbeitsort is made from Arbeit and Ort: the place where you work. Learn the plural of each word as you learn the word.

example.de: Im Rückblick war es eine gute Zeit.
example.en: Looking back, it was a good time.

cards.more: Picture a long road with signs. The road is the Werdegang: from the first job to today. The whole road with all its days is the Berufsleben. On the road there are hills, die Herausforderungen, and nice views, die Stärken. Sometimes you stumble: that is a Schwäche. A beginner at the start of the road is a Berufsanfänger. Where the road leads every morning is the Arbeitsort. At the end you look back: der Rückblick. One picture, ten words.

cards.title: Opening an interview politely
cards.body: Open an interview with Sie and three steps. First say thank you: Vielen Dank, dass Sie Zeit haben. Then ask permission: Darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen? Learn this question as one piece. Then ask a first question, for example Können Sie uns sagen, wie lange Sie schon Koch sind?
cards.lead: The ball game starts with a polite hello. This card gives you three set sentences for opening any interview, one of them with the indirect question from chapter 7.

deeper.text: Leon says uns because he asks for the whole club. If he asks only for himself, he says mir: Können Sie mir sagen, wo Ihr Restaurant ist? Both are polite. Use Sie with someone you do not know well or who is older, as Leon does with Herr Ali. The verb in the side sentence always goes to the end, here ist.

example.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wo Ihr Restaurant ist?
example.en: Can you tell me where your restaurant is?

cards.more: The opening is like knocking at a door before you enter. First you knock: Vielen Dank. Then you ask if you may come in: Darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen? Then you step in with the first question. A common slip is to keep the question word order inside the polite frame: Können Sie uns sagen, wie lange sind Sie Koch? That is wrong. After the comma the verb goes to the end: wie lange Sie Koch sind. Say the correct sentence aloud three times.

cards.title: Four kinds of questions
cards.body: A good interview mixes four kinds of questions. W-questions start with a question word: Wann haben Sie angefangen? Yes/no questions start with the verb: Waren Sie schon immer Koch? Was für questions ask for the kind: Was für ein Restaurant ist „Zum Löwen“? Indirect questions start with Können Sie uns sagen, … and end with the verb.
cards.lead: You have met all four question types separately. This card puts them side by side, so you can choose the right one for what you want to know.

examples.en: When did you start?
Have you always been a cook?

examples.en: What kind of restaurant is „Zum Löwen“?
examples.why: Was für: asks for the kind.

deeper.text: In an indirect question the question word stays, but the verb moves to the end. Direct: Warum kochen Sie gern? Indirect: Können Sie uns sagen, warum Sie gern kochen? The indirect form sounds more polite and fits an interview. A real interview mixes both: start with polite indirect questions and keep short direct ones for a quick follow-up.

example.de: Können Sie uns sagen, warum Sie gern kochen?
example.en: Can you tell us why you like cooking?

cards.more: Four tools in a toolbox. The W-question is a hammer: you ask for a detail and bang, you get it. The yes/no question is a switch: on or off. The Was für question is a ruler: it measures the kind. The indirect question is a soft glove: same job, but polite. A good interviewer picks the right tool at the right time. Try to write one question with each tool about your own life, then say them aloud.

cards.title: Answering about the past
cards.body: Answer in the Perfekt and use a time phrase. Vor 25 Jahren habe ich als Koch angefangen. After a time phrase the verb stays in second place: the subject comes after it. Seit 2010 habe ich ein Restaurant. Earlier work in the past with a modal: Früher musste ich viel arbeiten.
cards.lead: The questions are ready, now the answers. This card shows how to answer about your past with vor and seit and why the verb stays in second place even when a time phrase starts the sentence.

examples.de: Vor 25 Jahren habe ich als Koch angefangen.
examples.en: I started as a cook 25 years ago.
I have had a restaurant since 2010.
examples.why: seit: it is still true today.

examples.en: In the past I had to work a lot.

deeper.text: English and German differ here. English says I have had a restaurant since 2010, with a past form. German simply uses the present: Seit 2010 habe ich ein Restaurant. The thing is still true, so German stays in the present. Learners sometimes say Seit 2010 habe ich ein Restaurant gehabt, but that is not natural: the Perfekt would sound as if it were over. Same with learning: Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch.

example.de: Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch.
example.en: I have been learning German for two years.

cards.more: Imagine a timeline on the wall. A pin at the left says: vor 25 Jahren, the start. A pin in the middle says: seit 2010, the restaurant. The line runs up to today. Each pin begins a sentence, and then comes your verb in second place, like a train that always stops at the second station. So: Vor 25 Jahren habe ich angefangen. Seit 2010 habe ich ein Restaurant. Do not move the subject in front of the verb after a time phrase. Say each sentence with your own dates.

cards.title: Strengths, challenges and a tip
cards.body: Interviews often ask for strengths and weaknesses. Start with Meine Stärke ist … or Meine Schwäche ist … A challenge: Eine Herausforderung war … And end with a tip: Mein Tipp für Berufsanfänger: Sie sollten … With Sie sollten you give polite advice, as in lesson 2.
cards.lead: You can open, ask and answer about the past. This card adds the typical last part of an interview: strengths, a challenge and a tip with sollten from lessons 1 to 3.

examples.en: A challenge was the work in the evening.

examples.de: Mein Tipp für Berufsanfänger: Sie sollten viel fragen.

deeper.text: After Meine Stärke ist you can put a noun or a dass clause: Meine Stärke ist das Team. Meine Stärke ist, dass ich schnell arbeite. The dass clause has the verb at the end. For a tip to a beginner use Sie sollten, because the beginner may be a stranger. Between friends you say du solltest.

example.de: Meine Schwäche ist, dass ich nie Zeit habe.
example.en: My weakness is that I never have time.

cards.more: A strength is like a tool you carry in your bag, a weakness like a tool you forgot at home. Both are normal. In an interview you say them calmly, with a short sentence: Meine Stärke ist … Meine Schwäche ist … A challenge is a hill you climbed: Eine Herausforderung war … And a tip is the little gift at the end: Mein Tipp: Sie sollten … Practise four short sentences about yourself and say them aloud. Make them honest and short.

cards.title: The interview text and reporting it
cards.body: Read the whole interview in the table. Then report it. Use the Perfekt of the reporting verb and a side clause: Herr Ali hat erzählt, dass … or Leon hat gefragt, ob … The finite verb of the side clause goes to the end. Every question word is kept: Leon hat gefragt, was für ein Restaurant das ist.
cards.lead: This last card pulls the lesson together: one complete interview between Leon and Herr Ali, and then the same content told by someone else, with dass and ob, as you learned in chapter 7.

examples.en: Herr Ali said that career starters should ask a lot.

deeper.text: Use ob for yes/no questions and dass for statements. Leon asked a yes/no question: Waren Sie schon immer Koch? Reported: Leon hat gefragt, ob Herr Ali schon immer Koch war. The tense of the side clause can stay the same as in the original, so you need no new rule. Hear it once more in the dialogue before you try your own report.

example.de: Leon hat gefragt, ob Herr Ali schon immer Koch war.
example.en: Leon asked whether Herr Ali had always been a cook.

cards.more: Reporting is like passing a message. Anna was not at the interview. Leon tells her: Herr Ali hat erzählt, dass er vor 25 Jahren als Koch angefangen hat. Leon puts what was said in a side clause. Two small helpers do the job: dass for a statement and ob for a yes/no question. The verb goes to the end of the clause.
