grammar.point: At the end of a word or syllable, b sounds like p, d like t and g like k: Hund [t], Tag [k], gelb [p], Abendkurs [t]. When a vowel follows, the sound is soft again: Hunde, Tage. A word ending in -ig sounds like ich: wichtig. The spelling never changes. Give tips with Sie sollten / ihr solltet / du solltest + infinitive at the end.

mistake.why: You hear a t at the end, but the spelling keeps the d. The plural Hunde shows you the real letter.

terms.meaning: b, d, g at the end of a word sound like p, t, k (Auslautverhärtung)
one beat of a word: A-bend-kurs has three syllables
word ending that sounds like ich: wichtig, richtig

cards.title: Before we start: a club where neighbours help
cards.body: Frau Weber runs a club where neighbours help each other: „Viertel hilft“. You already know Verein, Mitglied and how to give advice with sollte. Today you read the club notice, and you learn why Hund ends with a t-sound, Tag with a k-sound and wichtig with ich.
steps: You already know: Ich bin Mitglied in einem Verein from chapter 6, and advice with du solltest … from this chapter.
New today: the club „Viertel hilft“, its words, and how b, d and g sound at the end of a word.
By the end you can: read a club notice, give advice to a new helper and say Hund, Tag and wichtig like a German.

examples.de: Ich bin Mitglied in einem Verein.
examples.en: I am a member of a club.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist Mitglied bei „Viertel hilft“.
examples.en: Frau Weber is a member of „Viertel hilft“.
examples.why: New today: a neighbourhood help club.

examples.de: Der Hund von der Nachbarin ist lieb.
examples.en: The neighbour's dog is sweet.
examples.why: New today: Hund is spelt with d, but you say a t at the end.

cards.more: Think of a street where people know each other. Someone carries the shopping for an older neighbour, someone else walks a dog. In German towns many people do this in small help groups. Today you meet one: „Viertel hilft“. You read its notice and give tips to new helpers with sollte. On the way you also train your ear: German b, d and g turn hard at the very end of a word. The spelling stays the same, only the sound changes. Step by step, one card at a time.

cards.title: Club words: „Viertel hilft“
cards.body: „Viertel hilft“ is a Nachbarschaftshilfe: neighbours help neighbours. The helpers work ehrenamtlich: they get no money. On the Aushang (notice) you read the Hilfsangebote, for example Einkaufshilfe for a Rentnerin. Nobody wants a Gegenleistung. The Treffpunkt is „Zum Löwen“ every Monday.
cards.lead: You know Verein and Mitglied from chapter 6. Now you get the words of one special club: a neighbourhood help group and the notice it puts up in the street.

examples.en: „Viertel hilft“ is a neighbourhood help group.
Frau Weber works as a volunteer (without pay).

examples.de: Der Treffpunkt ist jeden Montag im Restaurant „Zum Löwen“.
examples.en: The meeting point is „Zum Löwen“ every Monday.
The members support a pensioner.

deeper.text: Ehrenamt is built from Ehre (honour) and Amt (post, office): a post you do for honour, not for money. The adjective is ehrenamtlich. In many towns in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, neighbours run help groups like this. People say ohne Gegenleistung: you help and want nothing back.

example.de: Die Mitglieder helfen ohne Gegenleistung.
example.en: The members help without anything in return.

cards.more: Picture the board in the entrance of „Zum Löwen“. On it hangs a sheet of paper: that is der Aushang. On the sheet you read the Hilfsangebote: Einkaufshilfe on Tuesday, help with letters on Thursday. Below it says: Treffpunkt Montag, 18 Uhr. Who helps? Neighbours, ehrenamtlich, so for no money and without a Gegenleistung. Who gets help? For example a Rentner or a Rentnerin who cannot carry heavy bags. Now you can read the whole notice word by word.

cards.title: b, d, g at the end sound like p, t, k
cards.body: At the very end of a word, German b, d and g become hard: b sounds like p, d like t, g like k. So Hund sounds like [hunt], Tag like [taak], gelb like [gelp]. The spelling never changes: you still write b, d and g.
cards.lead: The club words had many endings like Hund and Treffpunkt. Now you learn the sound rule behind them: three letters that change their sound at the end of a word.

examples.de: Am Abend fährt der Zug ab.
examples.en: In the evening the train leaves. (Abend, Zug: t, k)

examples.de: Der Weg zum Berg ist lang.
examples.en: The way to the mountain is long. (Weg, Berg: k)
The dog is half yellow. (Hund: t; halb, gelb: p)

deeper.text: English keeps the voice at the end: dog, bad, cab. German switches it off. That is why Rad (bike) and Rat (advice) sound exactly the same: [raat]. Und also ends with a t-sound. The rule is called Auslautverhärtung (hardening at the end). You hear it in every sentence, so it is worth training.

example.de: Wir fahren am Abend mit dem Rad.
example.en: We ride the bike in the evening. (Abend, Rad: t)

cards.more: Put two fingers on your throat and say a long zzz. You feel a hum: that is a voiced sound. Now say sss: no hum. B, d and g normally hum. At the very end of a German word, the hum switches off, and they come out as p, t and k. English keeps the hum: dog ends with a soft g. German Tag ends with a hard k. Spelling does not change at all. Only your mouth does.
steps: Look at the last letter of the word.
Is it b, d or g? Say p, t or k.
Write it as normal: b, d or g.

cards.title: An ending brings the soft sound back
cards.body: When a vowel comes after b, d or g, they are soft again: Hund [t] but Hunde [d], Tag [k] but Tage [g]. Inside a long word, b, d and g are hard at the end of a syllable: Abend|kurs, täg|lich, Zug|fahrt, er gibt, er sagt.
cards.lead: You know the hard sound at the end of a word. This card shows when the soft sound comes back: with an ending, and when it is not the end of a syllable.

examples.en: The dogs play in the park. (Hunde: soft d)
Leon has an evening class. (Abend|kurs: t)
Leon gives the dog water. (gibt: p, Hund: t)
The paths are long. (Wege: soft g)

deeper.text: A syllable is one beat of a word. Clap Abendkurs: A-bend-kurs. The d closes the beat bend, so it is hard. In Hunde you clap Hun-de: the d opens a new beat, so it is soft. The same is true for verbs: er lobt [p], er sagt [k], but wir loben [b], wir sagen [g].

example.de: Wir sagen danke.
example.en: We say thank you. (sagen: soft g; er sagt: k)

cards.more: Think of the letter as a light switch. If the word stops right after b, d or g, the switch goes off: hard sound. If a vowel follows, the switch stays on: soft sound. Hund off, Hunde on. Tag off, Tage on. Gelb off, gelbe on. Long words have little stops inside them too: clap A-bend-kurs and you feel the d close a beat, so it is hard. When in doubt, clap the word and listen to where each beat ends.

cards.title: -ig at the end sounds like ich
cards.body: When a word ends in -ig, the course says it like ich: wichtig [wichtich], richtig, ruhig, fertig, lustig. With an ending the g is soft again: eine wichtige Frage [g]. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people often say [ik]; both are fine.
cards.lead: The hard g gives you the k-sound. One group of words is special: words that end in -ig. This short card shows the extra rule for them.

examples.en: That is important. (-ig: ich)
I am finished. (-ig: ich)
That is an important question. (wichtige: soft g)

deeper.text: One exception sounds odd but is useful: when -ig is followed by -lich, the g becomes k, because ich-lich would be hard to say. So königlich sounds like könik-lich. Everywhere else the -ig rule stays: billig, ruhig, wichtig all end in the ich-sound, and with a consonant after it too: er ist beruhigt [icht]. With a vowel after it, the g comes back.

example.de: Das Zimmer ist ruhig und billig.
example.en: The room is quiet and cheap.

cards.more: Imagine every -ig at the end hides a tiny ich. Wichtig sounds like wich-tich, richtig like rich-tich, fertig like fer-tich. It is a soft hiss, like when you say ich. When an ending follows, the g comes back as a real g: eine wichtige Frage, die richtige Antwort. In Bavaria, Austria or Switzerland you will hear wichtik with a k, and that is normal there. For this course, pick the ich-sound and use it every time.

cards.title: Advice for new helpers
cards.body: New helpers ask: what should I do? Give advice with sollte (Sie sollten …, ihr solltet …) or more directly with the imperative (Lesen Sie …!). Then read the practice sentence aloud: it is full of b, d and g at the end.
cards.lead: You can now say b, d and g at the end. Put it to work: give tips to new club helpers with sollte and the imperative, and read a sound-rich sentence aloud.

examples.en: You should read the notice.

examples.de: Ihr solltet am Montag zum Treffpunkt kommen.
examples.en: You (all) should come to the meeting point on Monday.
Read the notice!

examples.de: Am Abend geht Anna mit dem Hund den Weg zum Treffpunkt.
examples.en: In the evening Anna walks a neighbour's dog along the way to the meeting point.

deeper.text: For walking a dog, den Hund ausführen is correct, but in everyday speech people more often say mit dem Hund Gassi gehen or mit dem Hund rausgehen. Gassi gehen is a fixed phrase only for dogs, and Gassi never changes. On the club notice you might read: Gassi gehen für Rentner, and that is a very typical Hilfsangebot. Listen again for the hard d in Hund.

example.de: Anna geht mit dem Hund von einer Nachbarin Gassi.
example.en: Anna takes a neighbour's dog for a walk.

cards.more: Think of two keys for one door. The soft key is the tip: Sie sollten den Aushang lesen. It sounds friendly, like a suggestion from a neighbour. The strong key is the imperative: Lesen Sie den Aushang! It sounds like an instruction on a form. In a club you mostly use the soft key with new people. Then train your mouth with the long practice sentence: Abend, Hund and Weg all end hard, so say t, t and k, and read it three times.

cards.title: Anna wants to help
cards.body: Anna reads the Aushang and talks to Frau Weber. She wants to help. Frau Weber asks what she can do and tells her about a Rentner who needs Einkaufshilfe. Read the six lines aloud and listen for the hard ends.
cards.lead: Words, sounds and advice are ready. Now you see them in a real talk: Anna offers help, and Frau Weber explains what a neighbour needs.

examples.en: I would like to help at „Viertel hilft“.

examples.de: Was für eine Hilfe braucht er?
examples.en: What kind of help does he need?

examples.de: Sie sollten am Montag zum Treffpunkt kommen.
examples.en: You should come to the meeting point on Monday.

deeper.text: In many clubs members say du to each other quickly, even across ages. Frau Weber still says Sie to Anna, because they already know each other as neighbours with Sie, and changing needs an offer: Wollen wir uns duzen? Usually the older person offers it. Until then, both stay with Sie, even in a friendly club.

example.de: Wollen wir uns duzen?
example.en: Shall we say du to each other?

cards.more: Imagine you are Anna and you knock on Frau Weber's door. First you say what you want: Ich möchte helfen. Then Frau Weber asks when you have time, and you answer. Then she tells you what is needed: a Rentner needs an Einkaufshilfe. You ask Was für eine Hilfe? to get the details, and she ends with a tip: Sie sollten am Montag kommen. Read Anna's lines aloud, then read Frau Weber's lines, and listen for every hard end.

rows: Guten Tag, Frau Weber! Ich möchte bei „Viertel hilft“ helfen.
Ich habe am Abend Zeit. Ich kann einkaufen gehen.
Gut! Ein Rentner braucht eine Einkaufshilfe.
Was für eine Hilfe braucht er genau?
Er braucht Brot und Milch. Sie sollten am Montag zum Treffpunkt kommen.

lessons.title: Herr Ali lernt Italienisch: learning a language as an adult
lessons.goal: Understand and tell a learning story, tell past sollte from advice sollte, and give tips to adult learners.

grammar.topic: past sollte (was supposed to) and advice sollte (should); Präteritum modals and Perfekt in a story; man sollte
grammar.point: With a past time word (früher, als Kind, gestern) sollte is the Präteritum of sollen and means was supposed to. In a tip for now it is Konjunktiv II and means should. In a story use war, hatte and the modals in the Präteritum, and the Perfekt for other verbs: Er hat einen Kurs angefangen. Man sollte … gives a tip for everybody.
grammar.oneLine: Früher sollte er helfen. – Heute sollte er mehr sprechen.

mistake.wrong: Als Kind sollte ich mehr sprechen. (meaning: my tip for now)
mistake.why: With a past time word like als Kind, sollte means was supposed to. A tip for now needs a present context: heute, jetzt or no past time word.

terms.meaning: the short past: war, hatte, musste, sollte
the soft form for tips and wishes: du solltest, Sie könnten
people in general; takes the er/sie form of the verb

cards.title: Before we start: never too old to learn
cards.body: Herr Ali is over 50 and has started to learn Italian. Like you, he learns as an adult: with little time, a hard pronunciation and some fear of mistakes. You already tell the past with musste and wollte, and you give tips with sollte. Today you hear his story and learn when sollte means then and when it means now.
steps: You already know: Als Kind musste ich viel lernen (modals in the past, chapter 2) and Du solltest mehr üben (tips, this chapter).
New today: Herr Ali's learning story, words for language learning, and how to tell past sollte from advice sollte.
By the end you can: tell your own learning story and give tips to an adult learner.

examples.de: Als Kind musste ich viel lernen.
examples.en: As a child I had to learn a lot.
You should practise more.
examples.why: You know this already: a tip.

examples.de: Herr Ali lernt mit über 50 Italienisch.
examples.en: Herr Ali is learning Italian at over 50.
examples.why: New today: a learning story, then and now.

cards.more: Learning a language as an adult is like learning to ride a bike again after many years. You are slower at the start, but you know more about the world, and you can plan. Herr Ali shows how: a course, a tandem partner, ten minutes every day. On the way you meet a small trap. Sollte can look back (was supposed to) or give a tip (should). The time word tells you which one. You will practise both, card by card.

cards.title: Words for learning a language
cards.body: These words help you talk about learning: die Fremdsprache (a language that is not yours), die Aussprache, der Wortschatz (all the words you know), der Dialekt, die Geduld. A Lernpartner or a Tandem helps. Who learns well? People who are mutig. Some children are zweisprachig.
cards.lead: You meet Herr Ali, a learner like you. First you need the words for his story: words for language, for learning and for the people who learn.

examples.de: Italienisch ist eine Fremdsprache für Herrn Ali.
examples.en: Italian is a foreign language for Herr Ali.

examples.de: Die Aussprache ist schwer, aber Herr Ali ist mutig.
examples.en: The pronunciation is hard, but Herr Ali is brave.
The adults learn in the evening.
The child is bilingual.

deeper.text: Erwachsene comes from the adjective erwachsen (grown-up), so it changes like an adjective: die Erwachsenen (the adults), ein Erwachsener (an adult man), als Erwachsener or als Erwachsene (as an adult). Use these three chunks for now. Geduld has no plural: Geduld haben means to be patient.

example.de: Als Erwachsener lernt man anders.
example.en: As an adult you learn differently.

cards.more: Think of a backpack for a long walk. The Fremdsprache is the path you walk. The Wortschatz is the food in your bag: the more words, the further you get. The Aussprache is how your steps sound. A Dialekt is a side path that only some locals use. A Lernpartner or a Tandem walks next to you. Mutig means you keep walking even when you fall. And Geduld, patience, is the water bottle: without it, nobody gets far.

cards.title: Herr Ali's story
cards.body: Herr Ali tells his story. For the past he uses war, hatte and the modals (wollte, musste) in the Präteritum, and the Perfekt for everything else. Read the eight sentences and find the time words: als Kind, später, vor einem Jahr, am Anfang, jetzt.
cards.lead: You have the words. Now read how Herr Ali uses them in his own story, from his childhood to today, with the past forms you learned in chapter 2.

examples.de: Als Kind wollte er Sprachen lernen.
examples.en: As a child he wanted to learn languages.
He had to help in the restaurant.

examples.de: Vor einem Jahr hat er einen Kurs angefangen.
examples.en: A year ago he started a course.

deeper.text: Spoken German tells stories in the Perfekt: hat angefangen, hat gelernt. But for sein, haben and the modals people prefer the short Präteritum: war, hatte, wollte, musste, konnte. That is why Herr Ali's story mixes both. It is normal, not a mistake.

example.de: Am Anfang war die Aussprache schwer.
example.en: At the start the pronunciation was hard.

cards.more: Think of a photo album with five pages. Page one: als Kind, Herr Ali wanted to learn languages but had to help in the restaurant. Page two: später, lots of work. Page three: vor einem Jahr, a course at the Volkshochschule. Page four: am Anfang, hard pronunciation and many mistakes. Page five: jetzt, he understands a lot. Each page opens with a time word. Watch the Perfekt: Er hat gelernt, with ge- and -t, because lernen is regular.
steps: Als Kind wollte Herr Ali Sprachen lernen.
Aber er hatte keine Zeit: Er musste im Restaurant helfen.
Später hat er viel gearbeitet.
Vor einem Jahr hat er einen Italienischkurs an der Volkshochschule angefangen.
Am Anfang war die Aussprache schwer.
Er hatte wenig Geduld und hat viele Fehler gemacht.
Jetzt kann er schon viel verstehen und ein bisschen sprechen.
Er sagt: „Man ist nie zu alt.“

cards.title: sollte: then or now?
cards.body: Sollte has two meanings. With a past time word (früher, als Kind, gestern) it means was supposed to: a plan from the past. In a tip for now it means should: advice. The form looks the same, so look at the time word and the situation.
cards.lead: Herr Ali's story looks back, but his teacher gives tips for now. Both use sollte. This card shows you how to tell the two meanings apart.

examples.de: Früher sollte er jeden Tag in der Küche helfen.
examples.en: In the past he was supposed to help in the kitchen every day.

examples.de: Heute sagt die Kursleiterin: „Sie sollten mehr sprechen.“
examples.en: Today the course leader says: „You should speak more.“
You should practise every day.

deeper.text: Sollte has a third use you will see in letters and emails. At the very start of a sentence, with no wenn, it means if or in case: Sollten Sie Fragen haben, rufen Sie mich an. It is polite and a bit formal, typical for offices. You do not need to make these sentences yet, but now you will recognise them when you read them.

example.de: Sollten Sie Fragen haben, rufen Sie mich an.
example.en: If you have any questions, call me.

cards.more: Think of sollte as a coin with two sides. Side one looks back: Als Kind sollte er im Restaurant helfen. Someone gave him that job long ago. Side two looks at you: Sie sollten mehr sprechen. That is a tip for today. The coin looks the same on both sides, so you turn it over by checking the time words. Früher, als Kind, gestern: back. Heute, jetzt, no time word and a tip: now. English needs two phrases here; German uses one word.

rows: Als Kind sollte er im Restaurant helfen.

cards.title: Problems and tips for adult learners
cards.body: Adults often say: I have little time, the pronunciation is hard, I am afraid of mistakes. For each problem there is a tip with sollte. Read the problem on the left and the tip on the right, then make your own.
cards.lead: Now you can tell a past sollte from a tip. Use the tip meaning to help adults with three typical problems Herr Ali also had.

examples.en: I have little time.

examples.de: Sie sollten jeden Tag zehn Minuten üben.
examples.en: You should practise ten minutes every day.
You should read aloud.
You should be brave.

deeper.text: Why ten minutes a day? Memory works best with many short meetings, spread over days. Two hours on Sunday feel like hard work, but many words fade by Wednesday. Ten minutes daily keeps the words warm. That is why many adults learn on the bus or with a cup of coffee in the morning. Man sollte jeden Tag ein bisschen üben is the best tip of all.

example.de: Mein Tipp: Man sollte Geduld haben.
example.en: My tip: one should be patient.

cards.more: Picture a doctor's office for language learners. Patient one says: I have no time. The doctor: ten minutes a day. Patient two: the sounds are hard. Doctor: read aloud, every day. Patient three: I am afraid of mistakes. Doctor: be brave, mistakes are how you learn. Patient four: I forget words. Doctor: build an Eselsbrücke. Each prescription is one sollten sentence with the infinitive at the end. Now be the doctor for your own problem.

rows: Sie sollten jeden Tag zehn Minuten üben.

cards.title: A tandem in „Zum Löwen“
cards.body: Herr Ali has found a tandem partner: eine Nachbarin aus Rom from „Viertel hilft“. They meet in „Zum Löwen“. First they speak Italian for half an hour, then German. Each one teaches and each one learns, without money.
cards.lead: Tips are good, but a partner is better. Here Herr Ali finds a tandem partner, and you see how a tandem works.

examples.de: Herr Ali trifft eine Nachbarin aus Rom.
examples.en: Herr Ali meets a neighbour from Rome.

examples.de: Sie spricht Italienisch, er spricht Deutsch.
examples.en: She speaks Italian, he speaks German.

examples.de: Was für ein Tandem macht Herr Ali?
examples.en: What kind of tandem does Herr Ali do?

examples.de: Er macht ein Tandem mit einer Nachbarin aus Rom.

deeper.text: A tandem is fair: you give one hour of your language and get one hour of the other. It is good for speaking and for real everyday words. A course is good for grammar. Many adults do both. You can find a partner at a club, at the Volkshochschule or online.

example.de: Am Montag sprechen sie eine halbe Stunde Italienisch.
example.en: On Monday they speak Italian for half an hour.

cards.more: A tandem is a bicycle for two. Both people pedal, so both move forward. Herr Ali gives half an hour of German, his neighbour gives half an hour of Italian. He helps her with letters, she helps him with pronunciation. Nobody pays money; the payment is the other language. That is why tandems are so popular in German cities. You can do the same: find someone who wants to learn your language and wants to teach you German.

cards.title: Your own learning story
cards.body: Now tell your story in four steps: since when you learn, what was hard at the start, what you can do now, and your tip with man sollte. Man means people in general, and it takes the er/sie form: man sollte.
cards.lead: You know Herr Ali's story and his tandem. Now it is your turn: four short steps turn your own learning into a little story with a tip at the end.

examples.de: Ich lerne seit drei Monaten Deutsch.

examples.de: Jetzt kann ich einen Aushang lesen.

examples.de: Mein Tipp: Man sollte jeden Tag üben.

deeper.text: Do not mix man and der Mann. Man with one n means people in general, like English you or one in Man ist nie zu alt. Der Mann with two n is a man. Man is always small inside a sentence and always takes the er/sie form: man lernt, man sollte, man kann. Germans use man much more often than English uses one.

example.de: Man lernt nie aus.
example.en: You never stop learning.

cards.more: Think of four boxes in a row. Box one: Seit wann? Ich lerne seit drei Monaten Deutsch. Box two: Was war schwer? Am Anfang war die Aussprache schwer. Box three: Was kannst du jetzt? Jetzt kann ich einen Aushang lesen. Box four: your tip for others, with man sollte. Fill each box with one short sentence about your real life. Four true sentences are already a little story you can tell in a course or at a tandem meeting.

lessons.title: Meine Präsentation: prepare a presentation
lessons.goal: Prepare and give a short presentation of two or three minutes with clear opening, middle and closing sentences, and answer a question.

grammar.topic: presentation chunks; zuerst, dann, zum Schluss with the verb in position 2; tips with sollte
grammar.point: Open with Ich möchte euch/Ihnen heute … vorstellen (vorstellen at the end) or Mein Thema ist … Give the plan with zuerst, dann and zum Schluss: the verb stays in position 2 (Zuerst spreche ich über …). In the middle use Auf dieser Folie sehen Sie … and Jetzt komme ich zu … Close with Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass … and Vielen Dank für Ihre Aufmerksamkeit.

mistake.right: Zuerst spreche ich über den Verein.
mistake.why: Zuerst takes position 1, so the verb (spreche) must come second and the subject (ich) comes after it.

cards.title: Before we start: from a text to a talk
cards.body: Anna will present „Viertel hilft“ to her German course. Two or three minutes, people looking at her: that is exciting and a bit scary. You already plan a text with Einleitung, Hauptteil and Schluss and connect ideas with zuerst, dann and zum Schluss. Today you turn that plan into a spoken presentation.
steps: You already know: Einleitung – Hauptteil – Schluss from chapter 4, and zuerst, dann, zum Schluss with the verb in position 2.
New today: five steps to prepare a talk, and ready-made sentences for the start, the middle and the end.
By the end you can: give a short presentation of two or three minutes and answer a question.

examples.en: First I write the introduction.

examples.de: Ich möchte euch heute „Viertel hilft“ vorstellen.
examples.en: Today I would like to present „Viertel hilft“ to you.
examples.why: New today: a sentence to open a presentation.

cards.more: A presentation is a text you carry in your head instead of on paper. You already know how to build a text: a start, a middle and an end. A talk has the same three rooms, plus a few doors between them: sentences like Mein Thema ist … or Jetzt komme ich zu … They tell the listeners where you are. You also learn five steps to prepare, so you feel calm on the day. One card at a time, and Anna shows you a full example at the end.

cards.title: Words for a presentation
cards.body: A Präsentation or a Vortrag is a talk in front of a Publikum. On each Folie you write only Stichpunkte, not full sentences. The Gliederung is your plan: start, middle, end. Some speakers give out a Handout. You choose a Thema, you vorbereiten (prepare) and then präsentieren.
cards.lead: You know how to plan a written text. Before you can turn it into a talk, you need the words: what you show, what you prepare and who listens.

examples.en: Anna is preparing a presentation.

examples.de: Auf der Folie stehen nur Stichpunkte.
examples.en: There are only bullet points on the slide.
The audience has many questions.
My topic is neighbourhood help.

deeper.text: Vortrag and Präsentation are almost the same. A Vortrag is often longer and without slides, like a talk at a university. Präsentation sounds more like work or school, with Folien. Vorbereiten is separable: Ich bereite die Präsentation vor. In the Perfekt: Ich habe die Präsentation vorbereitet.

example.de: Ich habe die Folien vorbereitet.
example.en: I have prepared the slides.

cards.more: Picture a small stage in your German course. You stand at the front with a Thema, your topic. Behind you, a screen shows a Folie, a slide, with three Stichpunkte, only key words. In your hand is the Gliederung, your plan with start, middle and end. In front of you sits the Publikum, the audience, maybe holding your Handout. Before the day you vorbereiten, prepare; on the day you präsentieren. One stage, ten words, and you can name everything you see.

cards.title: Five steps to prepare
cards.body: Good speakers prepare in five steps. First choose a topic, then collect key words, then make a plan. After that make the slides. At the end practise aloud and check the time. Tips with sollte help: Du solltest nur Stichpunkte auf die Folie schreiben.
cards.lead: Now you have the words. This card puts them in order: five steps from an empty page to a talk you can give, with a sollte tip for each one.

examples.en: First you choose a topic.

examples.de: Du solltest nur Stichpunkte auf die Folie schreiben.
examples.en: You should write only bullet points on the slide.

examples.de: Zum Schluss solltest du die Präsentation laut üben.
examples.en: At the end you should practise the presentation aloud.

deeper.text: Why only Stichpunkte? Because the listeners read faster than you speak. With full sentences on the slide they read and stop listening. Three to five key words per slide is enough. And practise aloud with a clock: two minutes feel long in your head, but short on the stage.

example.de: Ihr solltet nicht zu schnell sprechen.
example.en: You (all) should not speak too fast.

cards.more: Think of cooking for friends. Step one, choose the dish: ein Thema wählen. Step two, buy what you need: Stichpunkte sammeln. Step three, read the recipe in order: eine Gliederung machen. Step four, put it on a nice plate: Folien machen, with only key words. Step five, taste it before the guests arrive: laut üben und die Zeit messen. If you skip step five, the dish surprises you on stage. Each step can become a tip with solltest.
steps: Ein Thema wählen.
Stichpunkte sammeln.
Eine Gliederung machen: Anfang, Mitte, Schluss.
Folien machen: nur Stichpunkte!
Laut üben und die Zeit messen.

cards.title: Starting your talk
cards.body: The first sentences tell the listeners what comes. Say your topic: Mein Thema ist … or Ich möchte euch heute … vorstellen. Then give the plan: Zuerst spreche ich über …, dann über … und zum Schluss über … After zuerst, dann and zum Schluss the verb comes second.
cards.lead: Your talk is prepared. Now you need its first sentences. This card gives you three chunks that open a presentation and show your plan.

examples.de: Ich möchte euch heute „Viertel hilft“ vorstellen.
examples.en: Today I would like to present „Viertel hilft“ to you.
My topic is neighbourhood help.

examples.de: Zuerst spreche ich über den Verein, dann über die Mitglieder.
examples.en: First I talk about the club, then about the members.

deeper.text: Use euch for friends and classmates, Ihnen for people you say Sie to: Ich möchte Ihnen heute … vorstellen. In the plan sentence you say spreche ich only once; after dann and zum Schluss you can just add über … That keeps it short and clear for the ear.

example.de: Ich möchte Ihnen heute unseren Verein vorstellen.
example.en: Today I would like to present our club to you.

cards.more: The start of a talk is like the map at the entrance of a park. First the name of the park: Mein Thema ist … Then the paths: zuerst, dann, zum Schluss. Listeners relax when they know the route. Watch two things. In Ich möchte euch heute … vorstellen, vorstellen waits at the very end, as after every modal. And after zuerst, the verb comes second: Zuerst spreche ich, never Zuerst ich spreche. Learn these three openers by heart.

rows: Ich möchte euch heute „Viertel hilft“ vorstellen.
Zuerst spreche ich über …, dann über …, zum Schluss über …
Zuerst spreche ich über den Verein, dann über die Hilfsangebote, zum Schluss über den Treffpunkt.

cards.title: The middle: show and move on
cards.body: In the middle you show your points and move from one to the next. Point at a slide: Auf dieser Folie sehen Sie … Stress a point: Das ist ein wichtiger Punkt. Give an example: Ein Beispiel: … Move on: Jetzt komme ich zu …
cards.lead: Your listeners know the plan. Now you walk them through it. These four chunks show a slide, stress a point, give an example and move to the next part.

examples.de: Auf dieser Folie sehen Sie den Treffpunkt.
examples.en: On this slide you see the meeting point.
That is an important point.

examples.de: Jetzt komme ich zu den Hilfsangeboten.
examples.en: Now I come to the offers of help.

examples.de: Ein Beispiel: Anna macht die Einkaufshilfe.
examples.en: An example: Anna does the shopping help.

deeper.text: Jetzt komme ich zu … works like a door: the listeners hear that one part ends and the next one starts. Zu takes the dative: zu dem Treffpunkt becomes zum Treffpunkt, zu der Gliederung becomes zur Gliederung. With friends say seht ihr: Auf dieser Folie seht ihr …

example.de: Jetzt komme ich zum Treffpunkt.
example.en: Now I come to the meeting point.

cards.more: The middle is a guided walk through a museum. At each picture you stop and point: Auf dieser Folie sehen Sie … You tell people why it matters: Das ist ein wichtiger Punkt. You give a small story: Ein Beispiel: … Then you walk to the next room: Jetzt komme ich zu … Without these signs the listeners get lost, just like visitors without a guide. Four small chunks are enough to sound clear and organised, even with simple A2 German.

cards.title: The end and questions
cards.body: At the end, sum up: Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass … Then open the floor: Habt ihr Fragen? or Haben Sie Fragen? Say thank you: Vielen Dank für eure/Ihre Aufmerksamkeit (attention). For a question say Gute Frage! If you do not know: Das weiß ich leider nicht genau.
cards.lead: You walked through the middle. Now close the talk well: one summary sentence, an invitation for questions, a thank-you, and two answers for when a question comes.

examples.de: Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass Helfen Spaß macht.
examples.en: Finally I would like to say that helping is fun.
Do you have any questions?
Thank you for your attention.

examples.de: Das weiß ich leider nicht genau.
examples.en: Unfortunately I don't know that exactly.

deeper.text: Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass … opens a dass-clause, so the verb goes to the end. Gute Frage! is a fixed chunk: it gives you a second to think. Die Aufmerksamkeit (attention) is a long word, but you need it only in this one thank-you sentence.

example.de: Gute Frage! Das weiß ich leider nicht genau.
example.en: Good question! Unfortunately I don't know that exactly.

cards.more: The end of a talk is like saying goodbye at the door. One last important sentence: Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass … Then you open the door for questions: Habt ihr Fragen? And you say thank you: Vielen Dank für eure Aufmerksamkeit. If a question comes that you cannot answer, do not panic. Gute Frage! buys you a second, and Das weiß ich leider nicht genau is honest and polite. A clear I don't know is fine in a talk.

rows: Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen, dass …
Habt ihr Fragen? / Haben Sie Fragen?
Gute Frage! / Das weiß ich leider nicht genau.

cards.title: Anna presents „Viertel hilft“
cards.body: Here is Anna's whole presentation. Find the three parts: Einleitung (topic and plan), Hauptteil (three points) and Schluss (summary, questions, thank you). Before she starts she has Lampenfieber (stage fright), so she uses some sollte tips.

deeper.text: Lampenfieber is normal, even for good speakers. Three tips help: Du solltest langsam sprechen. Du solltest vorher ein Glas Wasser trinken. Du solltest die ersten zwei Sätze auswendig können. Auswendig means by heart. If the start goes well, the rest follows.

example.de: Du solltest langsam sprechen.
example.en: You should speak slowly.

cards.more: Anna's talk is a house with three rooms. The front door is the Einleitung: hello, topic, plan. The three rooms in the middle are the Hauptteil: what the club is, what it offers, where it meets. The back door is the Schluss: one last sentence, questions, thanks. Read the talk twice and point at each room as you go. Then build your own house with a topic you know well, like your German course or your job.

reading.text:
Neu an der Volkshochschule
Italienisch lernen? Es gibt drei Kurse.
Kurs 1 ist ein Abendkurs für Anfänger. Er ist am Montag. Der Kurs ist nicht groß: Es gibt nur zehn Teilnehmer. Sie arbeiten mit einem Lehrbuch.
Kurs 2 ist ein Kurs für Fortgeschrittene. Er ist am Mittwoch. Die Kursleiterin kommt aus Rom.
Kurs 3 ist ein Online-Kurs. Die Teilnehmer lernen mit der Lernplattform. Jeder braucht nur einen Computer. Zuerst macht jeder einen Einstufungstest.
Nachricht von Anna:
Hallo Herr Ali, ich mache jetzt den Abendkurs für Anfänger. Was für einen Kurs suchen Sie? Sie lernen schon seit einem Jahr Italienisch. Der Kurs für Fortgeschrittene ist gut für Sie, und am Mittwoch haben Sie Zeit.
Viele Grüße
Anna

reading.text:
Der Aushang von „Viertel hilft“

Brauchen Sie Hilfe? Wir helfen gern! „Viertel hilft“ ist eine Nachbarschaftshilfe. Unsere Mitglieder arbeiten ehrenamtlich und ohne Gegenleistung.

Unsere Hilfsangebote:
– Einkaufshilfe: Wir gehen für Sie einkaufen.
– Hund: Wir führen Ihren Hund am Abend aus.
– Deutsch im Tandem: Sie lernen mit einem Lernpartner.

Treffpunkt: jeden Montag um 18 Uhr im Restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Fragen? Rufen Sie Frau Weber an!

Eine Notiz von Herrn Ali:
Seit einem Monat mache ich ein Tandem mit einer Nachbarin aus Rom. Am Montag sprechen wir eine halbe Stunde Deutsch und eine halbe Stunde Italienisch. Die Aussprache ist schwer, aber ich habe Geduld. Mein Tipp: Man sollte keine Angst vor Fehlern haben.

Viele Grüße
Herr Ali
